## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Navigate the course: find any episode by its number, use the Overview and Key points cards, and track your own progress.
- Recognise every kind of box (note, pitfall, predict, bridge, deep dive, exercise, checkpoint) and know what each one asks of you.
- Run Python code either in Google Colab with nothing installed, or in a local environment built from `environment.yml` or `requirements.txt`, and confirm it works with `scripts/check_env.py`.
- Judge honestly whether your Python is ready for Chapter 1, and know where to brush up if it is not.
:::

## Schedule

{{< generated ch00-schedule >}}

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
Nothing, except one introductory programming course in any language and a willingness to type things in. If you have never written a loop or a function, do the [self-check](03-self-check.html) first; its closing section lists three free refreshers that will get you there in a week or two.
:::

## Suggested paths by background

The course is written for four kinds of graduate. Everyone reads the same episodes, but you will find different parts easy, and the *bridge* boxes (Chemist's corner, Biologist's corner, Maths corner, For programmers) are there to catch you where your background does not. The [maths refresher](../../appendices/maths-refresher.html) covers vector spaces and matrices, inner products and norms, derivatives and gradients, probability, sample statistics, and logarithms; the right column says which of those to skim before Chapter 2.

| Background | What will feel easy | Where to slow down | Skim first in the maths refresher |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Informatics / computer science** | Python, environments, notebooks, debugging. Chapter 1 will be quick; read it for the NumPy and pandas idioms rather than the syntax. | Chapter 2 onwards, where the *data* carry meaning. The chemistry and biology bridge boxes are not optional for you: a model is only as good as your grasp of what a solubility or an expression value actually measures. | Derivatives and gradients; probability; mean, variance and distributions. |
| **Chemistry** | The scientific questions. You already know why solubility, lipophilicity and molecular size matter, which is half of Chapter 2 and all of Part II. | Chapter 1. Take the full time on arrays, DataFrames and plots, and do every exercise; the code habits you build there carry the whole course. | Vectors, matrices and inner products; logarithms (logS and pKa are both base-10 logarithms, and the course leans on that). |
| **Biology** | Experimental design: blinding, replicates and controls are exactly the ideas behind test sets, cross-validation and baselines in Chapter 2. | Chapter 1, as for chemists, and the maths in the deep-dive boxes of Chapter 2. Open them: they are short and they explain *why* the methods work, not just how. | Probability; mean, variance and distributions; logarithms; then vectors and matrices. |
| **Mathematics** | Everything in the deep-dive boxes, and the linear algebra of Chapter 2. You will want the formal view early; the Maths corner boxes give it. | Chapter 1 for the tooling, and the parts of every chapter that are about data rather than theorems: units, missing values, what a dataset does and does not represent. | None needed. Instead read the reproducibility checklist at the end of [episode 2.6](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/06-pipelines-leakage.html) before Chapter 2, so that seeds and splits make sense from the start. |

Whatever your background, do the three episodes of this chapter in order. [Episode 0.1](01-how-this-course-works.html) takes ten minutes, [episode 0.2](02-setup.html) gives you somewhere to run code, and [episode 0.3](03-self-check.html) tells you whether to start Chapter 1 now or after a short refresher.
